knownGaps: Cancellation has no dedicated event. A user interrupt surfaces as session.error carrying error.name=MessageAbortedError, immediately followed by session.status{idle} and session.idle. An adapter that ignores the error name cannot tell a cancelled turn from a failed one: a provider auth failure emits the identical event shape with error.name=ProviderAuthError. The lane is correct either way because session.status is state-shaped; only the terminal outcome depends on reading the name.
Subagent activity has no dedicated event. Child sessions are identifiable only by info.parentID on session events.

The blocked lane is transition-shaped, not state-shaped: session.status only ever carried busy or idle, and blocking is visible solely as the permission.asked/permission.replied pair. A dropped permission.asked therefore does not self-correct the way a dropped busy/idle does.

tool.execute.after did not fire on 1.18.23 even though tool.execute.before did, so tool completion cannot be relied on as an event. The cancellation traces used a tool-free prompt and did not re-test this on 1.18.25.

Both ~/.config/opencode/plugin/ and ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ are loaded, and an asset present in both fires every event twice. The installer must own exactly one path and repair must detect the other.

Every export of a plugin module must be a plugin factory. One non-function export and the module is imported and then never called, silently and with no error. Measured on 1.18.25 with four probe plugins. This is invisible to offline tests: the plugin installs cleanly, its unit tests pass, and it reports nothing at all.

There is no event ordering guarantee across separate report processes. Reports must be serialized by the integration, because the lifecycle store enforces a strictly increasing sequence per run and correctly rejects an out-of-order arrival.
sourceVersionNote: Traced against opencode 1.18.23 (Phase A) and 1.18.25 (Phase B cancellation) on darwin/arm64, 2026-08-30. Docs page states no version or stability level; the hook interface was cross-read from packages/plugin/src/index.ts.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single SessionStart hook: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects. Codex's own contract is far broader and is now fully traced (see the next gap), so the ceiling here is what Sidecar ships rather than what Codex can do.

Codex's full lifecycle IS traced and would support the full tier once an adapter ships for it. Real captures on 0.151.0 cover work start (UserPromptSubmit), tool use (PreToolUse/PostToolUse), blocking (PermissionRequest, the last event before the pane blocks), unblocking (PostToolUse on approval), turn completion (Stop), cancellation (Interrupt, captured by two independent routes), session identity (SessionStart) and process exit (SessionEnd). Every event carries session_id and, from UserPromptSubmit onward, turn_id.

Four of the twelve events the shipped binary enumerates were NOT traced: SubagentStart, SubagentStop, PreCompact and PostCompact. The handoff says the evidence supports the full tier, and it does for every transition the promotion gate names — but the gate also names compaction and sub-agent isolation, and those rest on the binary's embedded schemas rather than on a capture. So it is unknown whether a sub-agent's events carry a distinguishing field the way Claude's agent_id does; if they do not, a sub-agent's tool calls are indistinguishable from the pane conversation's and would drive the pane's lane. opencode and pi both carry a sub-agent gap for the same reason, and Codex's silence about one was an omission rather than a clean bill of health.

Denying a permission request emits Interrupt, not PostToolUse and not Stop. Interrupt is therefore the universal 'the turn ended without completing' signal and the blocked lane always resolves; an adapter that treats only PostToolUse as the unblock would latch on blocked whenever a user says no.
SessionEnd does not fire under `codex exec` at all. It was observed only in the interactive TUI, so process exit on a non-interactive run is detectable only by process liveness.

No event re-asserts state. Unlike OpenCode's session.status, every Codex event is transition-shaped, so a dropped or missed event does not self-correct and an adapter cannot rely on the next event to repair the lane.

The trusted_hash is computed over the EFFECTIVE hook, after Codex clamps it, not over the hook as written. Codex clamps SessionEnd and Interrupt hook timeouts to 3s and prints a warning naming hooks.json on every start. A pre-written record for those two events at Sidecar's canonical timeout of 10 does not match, and the user gets the interactive 'Hooks need review' prompt. Proved by letting Codex write its own records and diffing them: the identity hashed with timeout=3 matches byte-for-byte and timeout=10 does not. Any lifecycle adapter must declare timeout<=3 on those two events.

Hooks are disabled by default behind features.hooks, so the integration must edit config.toml as well as hooks.json: three owned mutations (entry, feature flag, trust record) rather than one. Uninstall deliberately leaves features.hooks on, because other installed hooks may depend on it.

Codex only auto-runs hooks whose trusted_hash in config.toml matches a hash of the hook's normalized identity; an untrusted hook triggers an interactive 'Hooks need review' prompt. Sidecar pre-writes the record using the algorithm reproduced from codex-rs; it is now live-verified across eleven distinct event names in a single run rather than the one session_start vector, which is considerably stronger evidence that the reproduction is correct. It remains a provider implementation detail rather than a published contract, and if it drifts the failure mode is that visible one-time prompt, not a silent loss.

Trust records are keyed by the hook's position in hooks.json (path:event:group:hook). Any edit that reorders groups, by the user or by Sidecar removing its own group when others follow it, silently invalidates the trust records of the hooks that shifted, and Codex re-prompts for them.

config.toml is edited by a line writer with a TOML parser as its read-only oracle. A config.toml containing a genuine multi-line string (a structural triple-quote delimiter) is refused outright: install, repair and uninstall all decline rather than guess where a table header ends, so the integration is unavailable to a user whose config uses one. A delimiter appearing inside a comment or an ordinary single-line string no longer refuses. The scanner also declines any key = value line it cannot normalise, which is stricter than necessary. All of these fail in the safe direction.
The integration manages ~/.codex only; a CODEX_HOME override relocates the provider's configuration where the installer does not look.

Herdr shipped a full-lifecycle Codex hook set through eight asset versions and then deliberately removed it, retaining SessionStart for session identity only. Sidecar's own traces do not reproduce a reason for that rollback: every transition such a hook set needs is observable on 0.151.0. It stays recorded as unexplained rather than refuted, because a contract that held in one capture session is not the same as one that holds across versions.
sourceVersionNote: codex-cli 0.151.0 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-08-30 into an isolated CODEX_HOME with hooks that recorded event names only, on a private tmux socket; the user's real ~/.codex was never written. Traces are in testdata/traces/codex. The published config-reference URL redirects and truncates before the hooks section; the authoritative contract is codex-rs/app-server-protocol HookEventName plus the JSON schemas embedded in the shipped binary, which enumerate PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, UserPromptSubmit, Stop and Interrupt.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single SessionStart hook entry: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects.

Claude's lifecycle is traced and supports ADVISORY, not full. Real captures on 2.1.220 cover work start (UserPromptSubmit), tool use (PreToolUse/PostToolUse), blocking (PermissionRequest plus a Notification), turn completion (Stop), session identity (SessionStart) and process exit (SessionEnd). What is missing is a contract gap rather than a tracing gap; see below.

PermissionRequest DOES fire on the current release, correcting an earlier docs-only reading of this entry which held that session identity was all Claude offered. Blocking is first-class: PreToolUse, then PermissionRequest, then Notification, and then nothing at all until the user answers.

PostToolUse is silently skipped for any tool that went through the interactive permission prompt. The same tool with no prompt fires it normally. An adapter that unblocks on PostToolUse therefore unblocks on exactly the turns that never blocked, and never on the ones that did.

No user-cancellation event exists at all. Interrupting a live turn with Escape produced no hook event whatsoever: not Stop, and not any of the speculative event names Claude accepted into its settings without complaint. Denying a permission request, or Escape-cancelling the prompt, is equally silent. Because Stop does not fire either, a state machine driven only by these hooks latches on working or blocked forever. This is the single gap that caps Claude below full lifecycle authority, and no amount of further tracing can close it.
Stop means stopped generating, not ready for input, so turn completion cannot be taken from it without reconciliation against screen state.

Both halves of Herdr's stated reason for removing its own full-lifecycle Claude hook set, missed permission results and escape interrupts, are independently reproduced here on the current release. That rollback is now explained rather than merely recorded.

Hook configuration merges additively across five layers (enterprise, project, local, user, plugin), so Sidecar can own exactly its one entry in ~/.claude/settings.json and can never own the effective hook set; another layer can add, but not remove, hooks beside it.
The integration manages ~/.claude/settings.json only; a CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR override relocates the provider's configuration where the installer does not look.

grok reads hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json by design -- its shipped documentation carries a 'Claude Code Compatibility' section for exactly that -- so Sidecar's installed Claude entry also fires inside grok sessions. Because --kind is a flag rather than something checked against the pane's actual occupant, a grok session can be bound as kind=claude carrying grok's session identifier. Tracked as td-11040b.
sourceVersionNote: claude 2.1.220 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-08-30. Hooks were injected with the additive --settings flag and an isolated working directory, so nothing in the user's ~/.claude was written; the interactive half ran on a private tmux socket. Traces are in testdata/traces/claude. Recording captured event names and field names only, never any field value.

knownGaps: TRACED, and the tier is the ceiling the traces can reach. Four sanitized captures of pi 0.84.3 are in testdata/traces/pi: a successful turn, a turn that called a tool, a user cancellation, and a provider-error turn followed by /quit. They cover work start (agent_start), turn completion (agent_settled) and session identity (session_start with ctx.sessionFile present), which is exactly what the shipped asset reports and exactly what `covered` claims. `advisory` is the ceiling rather than a waypoint: `full` needs blocked_on_request and unblocked, and no released Pi can produce either.

The traces are what the asset's two invisible guards rest on, and they measure both. ctx.isIdle is FALSE on agent_end and TRUE on agent_settled three milliseconds later, so an asset that closed a turn on agent_end would report idle while Pi still considers the run active. And turn_start/turn_end fire TWICE inside one agent run when a tool is called -- once around the tool call, once around the reply -- so a turn in Pi's vocabulary is a provider round trip and turn_end is not turn completion either. agent_settled fires once, at the end. See traces/pi/simple-turn.tsv and traces/pi/tool-turn.tsv.

`sidecar agent start --kind pi` still times out, and the hooks lane cannot fix it. The tool turn ran a bash command with no permission event, so the pane is reachable; what refuses is the process gate. Pi installs as a `#!/usr/bin/env node` shim, tmux reports the pane's foreground command as `node`, and DetectPi returns pi.process-mismatch before any manifest rule is evaluated. The screen lane by itself answers idle for the same capture (`sidecar agent explain --file` gives state=idle, fallback_reason=default_known_agent_idle_fallback), so widening the process gate is the whole fix -- and that is the parity plan's Slice 3, not this one. No tier promotion reaches it either: agentcontrol's detector calls agentactivity.Detect only and never consults the lifecycle store.

The blocked lane is structurally unreachable, not merely untraced, so `full` can never be earned. Pi ships no permission system, so there is nothing to be blocked on. The only shape a Pi block could have is a cooperative extension-to-extension protocol on Pi's untyped event bus, which is what Herdr's asset listens for and what Sidecar's listens for on its own namespace -- and nothing publishes either channel. The string "herdr" does not appear in pi 0.84.3's shipped bundle at all; ExtensionAPI.on enumerates thirty events and not one is a permission, approval or prompt event; and Herdr's four occurrences of its own channel name are two listeners and two test drivers. The branch is kept and driven by a fixture so the ladder stays identical to upstream's, and the transition is not claimed. traces/pi/tool-turn.tsv adds the one thing a capture can add here: a bash tool runs unconditionally, with no permission, approval or prompt event anywhere between before_agent_start and agent_settled. It does NOT show anything about the untyped bus, because no column in that format observes one; the tracer listened on both channels and neither fired, but a fixture cannot tell that apart from never having subscribed, so the unreachability claim rests on the emitter-side reading above rather than on the capture.

Turn completion must come from agent_settled and never from agent_end. agent_end means "this attempt stopped" and Pi can follow it with an automatic retry or a compaction (_willRetryAfterAgentEnd, dist/core/agent-session.js:369), so an adapter that reported idle on it would announce a finished turn in the middle of one. The shipped asset does not subscribe to agent_end at all, and upstream's fixture asserts that absence directly.

process_exit is NOT claimed and the asset does not subscribe to session_shutdown. That event fires with reason quit, reload, new, resume or fork, so three of its five reasons are a session swap rather than an exit, and releasing the lane on those would hand a live pane back to screen detection mid-run. Sidecar already owns process liveness for every provider. The reason IS readable: the last row of traces/pi/error-turn-and-quit.tsv is session_shutdown carrying reason=quit, captured by typing /quit. So a future version that subscribed and released only on that reason could claim this; today it is unclaimed by choice, and this gap and `covered` move together when it changes.

tool_use is NOT claimed by choice, not by absence. tool_execution_start and tool_execution_end do fire and do carry toolName -- traces/pi/tool-turn.tsv records both around a bash call -- and the shipped asset subscribes to neither, because tool use is a refinement of work_start rather than a separate lane and every subscription is another event whose ordering has to be reasoned about.

Cancellation has no event, now measured rather than inferred. traces/pi/cancelled-turn.tsv is a turn interrupted with Escape; the pane printed "Operation aborted" and the event stream is byte-identical in shape to a completed turn -- turn_end, agent_end, agent_settled, same field names, nothing distinguishing. The listener stayed attached for 20s afterwards and nothing further arrived. agent_settled is emitted from a finally block, so the lane is still correct; only the terminal outcome is unknowable, which is why `cancelled` is not claimed.
There are no subagent events. An agent an extension spawns is a separate process, so nothing in Pi's event stream describes it and a parent's lane can never be derived from a child's.

The extension API publishes no version or stability guarantee, and Pi's changelog records breaking changes that have already shipped. An integration written against 0.84.3 has no contractual reason to keep working on 0.85 -- 0.84.4 was already offered as an update during the capture run -- which is why testedProviderRange is the single version actually driven and not a range.

Pi loads extensions from a project-local <cwd>/.pi/extensions as well as the user-level directory. Sidecar installs only into the user-level one: a per-project copy would follow a checkout into other people's clones and would report from panes Sidecar never set up.

PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR relocates Pi's whole agent directory, and OMP is a rebranded fork of the same codebase reading the same variable. With it set, Pi and OMP collapse onto one extension directory. Sidecar ships no OMP adapter yet, so nothing collides today; whichever adapter lands second has to refuse the collision the way Herdr's install_omp does.
sourceVersionNote: pi 0.84.3 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-09-02 against openrouter z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (and, for the error turn, the retired stealth/ox-alpha). The contract was first read from the released package's own dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts (the event set, ctx.mode, ctx.isIdle, sessionManager.getSessionFile/getSessionId), dist/core/agent-session.js (the settle ordering that makes the isIdle guard correct) and dist/config.js (PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR, tilde-expanded, defaulting to ~/.pi/agent, with extensions loaded from <that>/extensions); every load-bearing claim in it is now backed by a capture. The traces were taken from a live Pi TUI in a Sidecar-managed shell on a private tmux server, with PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR, XDG_STATE_HOME and -config all under a scratch tree and SIDECAR_ISOLATED_STATE=1; the user's real ~/.pi was never written. Sidecar's own asset was installed by `sidecar agent integration install pi` rather than by hand, and the hooks lane was proved end to end: the store recorded idle(session_start), working(turn_start), idle(turn_complete) from source sidecar.pi.extension with a session reference bound by path. The event mapping is ported from Herdr's pi integration at HERDR_INTEGRATION_VERSION=8; see internal/agentintegration/portedfrom.go.

Muse Spark 1.0.1 traced locally (darwin/arm64, echo provider) but hooks are not shipped: Muse Code's extension surface is skills, MCP servers, and the MSP wire schema, not lifecycle hooks. No published hook contract like Claude Code's hooks or Codex's hooks.json was found in the binary or docs at https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/.

The session log (JSONL at ~/.local/share/muse/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/<uuid>/session.jsonl) and SQLite index at ~/.local/share/muse/session-index.db are the durable stores; reasoning text is encrypted (encrypted_content) and tool call/result shapes are visible but not hook-authored.
Screen detection is therefore the sole lane authority; the capability entry exists so the provider appears in the matrix and can be promoted when and if Muse ships lifecycle hooks.

knownGaps: NOT TRACED. The adapter, the twelve hook entries and the installer ship, but no capture of a live Kimi Code CLI session backs any transition, so nothing is claimed and screen detection remains the sole authority. `covered` is empty on purpose: a tier is earned from traces of a released provider version and is never copied from Herdr's table, and Herdr gives kimi full lifecycle authority. Promoting this entry means capturing traces into testdata/traces/kimi and re-deriving each claim in hooktrace_test.go.

Session identity cannot be bound on this build, and the cause is in Sidecar rather than in Kimi. `sidecar agent report-session` canonicalises its --kind through agentcatalog.Lookup, which searches the launchable families and their aliases only; kimi is a detection-only family, so Lookup("kimi") is false and the SessionStart hook is refused with unsupported_kind. State reports are unaffected, because `agent report` checks --provider against the pane's resolved occupant instead and agentactivity identifies a kimi process by name. The SessionStart entry ships anyway: it is correct, it is inert rather than wrong, and it starts working the moment kimi becomes a family the catalog can resolve, which is Slice 5 of the parity plan.

Kimi runs every hook matching an event in parallel, so two rows matching one event would be two report processes racing for a store sequence. Upstream's table avoids it by construction -- the only doubled event is PreToolUse and its two matchers are exact complements -- and a row added later without a complementary matcher would reintroduce the race silently. TestKimiFiresExactlyOneHookPerEvent is the guard.

The PreToolUse working row uses upstream's negative-lookahead matcher `^(?!AskUserQuestion$).*$`, which Kimi's own regular-expression engine has to support. Kimi's published hooks reference documents `matcher` as "a regular expression" without naming the engine, so whether a lookahead compiles is untested here. If it does not, the failure is one missing working report on ordinary tool use, not a broken configuration: UserPromptSubmit still starts the turn and Stop still ends it.

process_exit is not claimed and SessionEnd is deliberately not hooked. Upstream's twelve rows do not include it, and this port keeps the provider half verbatim rather than adding knowledge Herdr does not have. Kimi does publish SessionEnd (with an exit/archive matcher target), so a future version that hooked it could claim the transition; today Sidecar owns process liveness for every provider anyway.

cancelled is reported as a lane but is not a terminal outcome. Interrupt maps to idle with reason `cancelled`, matching upstream's idle action; no `sidecar agent end --outcome cancelled` is sent, because a turn interrupt is not a run ending. StopFailure, which Kimi publishes for a failed turn, is likewise not hooked by upstream and not hooked here.

Sub-agent activity is visible only as SubagentStart, which upstream maps to working, and there is no SubagentStop row, so a sub-agent cannot return the pane to idle on its own. The turn's own Stop does that. Whether a sub-agent's PreToolUse events are distinguishable from the pane conversation's is unknown without a trace.

The integration manages one file, $KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml or ~/.kimi-code/config.toml. Kimi also reads a project-local .kimi-code/local.toml; Sidecar deliberately does not install there, because a per-project copy would follow a checkout into other people's clones and report from panes Sidecar never set up.

config.toml is edited by a line editor that only ever replaces the region between its own two marker comments, with a TOML parser as a read-only oracle at both ends of every edit. A config.toml containing a structural multi-line string is refused outright -- install, repair and uninstall all decline rather than risk a marker comment inside a string body -- so the integration is unavailable to a user whose config uses one. That fails in the safe direction.
sourceVersionNote: Not traced. The event contract was read from Kimi Code CLI's own published hooks reference (twenty events; a four-field [[hooks]] schema of event, matcher, command and timeout, where any extra field makes the whole config fail to load; a stdin payload carrying hook_event_name, session_id, session_title, client_type and cwd; and fail-open exit-code semantics) and from Kimi's configuration reference for $KIMI_CODE_HOME and ~/.kimi-code/config.toml. The event-to-lane mapping is ported row for row from Herdr's kimi integration at HERDR_INTEGRATION_VERSION=7, whose minimum supported Kimi Code is 0.14.0; see internal/agentintegration/portedfrom.go.
